seo.metaDescription: Build your own chart from Chart and its 18 building blocks: bars, lines, areas, axes, annotations, connectors, rows and tables.

props.markdown: Every chart in `tally-charts` is a `Chart` with marks inside it. `BarChart`, `LineChart` and the rest are ready-made arrangements of the same 18 building blocks, so when none of them fits, you arrange the blocks yourself.

`Chart` owns the data, the `x` and `y` scales, the size, the keyboard and pointer handling and the accessible name. The building blocks are its children: each one reads the scales from context and draws one thing, or adds one behavior. Order is paint order, so what comes first sits at the back.

Start with a band scale on `x` and a linear scale on `y`. `Grid` and `Axis` frame the plot, `Bars` draws the data, and `ValueLabel`, `Target`, `ColumnHighlight` and `Callout` say what to look at. `Tooltip` shows the hovered or focused bar.

`ColumnHighlight` and `Target` come before `Bars` so they sit behind it. `Callout` pins a pill to a point by `id`, so `Bars` is given `id="week"` and the callout points at `"W5"`. All the props here are strings, numbers and plain objects, which is why this example also renders in a Server Component.

A high-level chart renders its `children` after its own marks, so a building block you pass sits on top of the chart. A `Callout` lives in the HTML overlay: it appears after mount, is hidden from screen readers (put the same facts in the title, the description or the data), and never gets wider than the chart, wrapping instead.

`Target` also works on a band or point scale. Pass the category as `x` (or `y` on a horizontal chart) and `position`, a fraction of the category's step from 0 (start edge) to 1 (end edge); the default 0.5 is the centre. A pass mark of 73 over buckets 10 wide sits at `position={0.3}` of `"70–79"`. The end of one category and the start of the next are the same pixel, in the middle of the gap between bars. `position` on a linear or time scale warns and is ignored.

A point scale puts categories on a line. `Band` fills a range between a low and a high field, `Area` fades down from the line, and `Line` draws the path. `Region` shades a span of the x axis, here the forecast months. `NearestPointer` finds the point closest to the pointer, which is how a line chart gets its hover.

`Line` draws a path but does not register points, so on its own nothing can be hovered or reached with the arrow keys. `Dots` registers one point per dot, and `NearestPointer axis="x"` picks the column under the pointer. The dots need pixel positions, which is what the next section is about.

**Custom marks read the scales with `useChart()`.** It returns the resolved `x` and `y` scales and the chart size. Narrow on `x.kind` and `y.kind` (`linear`, `band`, `point` or `time`) before calling `scale`. A hook cannot run in a Server Component, so a file that defines such a mark starts with `'use client'`; so does a file that passes functions as props, like `DataTable` column readers or `Tooltip` `content`.

A value axis can run backwards. Where 1 is the best result, as with a search position or a league table, give `y` a descending domain: `y={{ domain: [10, 1] }}` on `Chart`, or `domain={[10, 1]}` on `LineChart`. Then 1 sits at the top, 10 at the bottom, and the line climbs as the result improves. `Axis`, `Grid`, `Line`, `Area`, `Band`, `Target`, the pointer and the arrow keys all follow the domain, and the arrow keys still step through the data in order. Explicit domains are never niced, so pick ends that suit the ticks.

`Bars` are the exception. A bar grows from the baseline, the domain value nearest zero, which on a reversed scale is the top edge: a bar for position 5 hangs from the top and is 4/9 of the plot tall, and a bar for position 1 has no length. That is consistent but rarely what a ranking wants, so use a line or dots for reversed scales.

`Bars` takes a `from` field: each bar then runs from `from` to its value instead of from zero, which makes floating steps. `Connector` draws the thin lines between neighbouring bars at the height where one step ends and the next begins.

`tone` takes a function per bar, so one `Bars` layer holds the totals, the gains and the losses. `ariaLabel` and `segments` report the change of each step instead of its end value, so the keyboard and screen readers walk the bridge left to right and hear "Costs, -30". Functions in props make this a client file.

Swap the axes and a band scale on `y` gives rows. `RowLabels` writes a name and an optional second line in the margin, `RowDividers` rules between the rows, and a small component of your own marks the plan on each row with `Dots` (the grey dots).

`DataTable` is the visually hidden table that gives screen-reader users the same numbers. A chart renders one from its `dataTable` prop; use the component directly when you build the table yourself. See [Getting started](/docs/getting-started) for why every chart needs a name, and [LineChart](/docs/line-chart) for what the ready-made line chart arranges for you.

The charts follow a few rules, so a prop that means one thing on one mark means the same on the next.

- `BarChart`'s `x` is the category and `y` the value, in both orientations.
- `at` is scoped by its mark: a data index (a number) on `ValueLabel`, a category on `ColumnHighlight` and a value on a `Connector` link.
- `radius` is the corner radius on `Bars` and `ColumnHighlight`, and the dot radius elsewhere.
- Numbers in data follow one rule: numbers and numeric strings count, while blanks, booleans and other values are missing.
- Toggles are bare booleans (`legend`, `totals`, `grid`, `tooltip`, …). Only `showValues` and `showScale` carry `show`, where the bare word would be ambiguous.
- `meta` is a number on a `WaterfallStep` and an accessor on `RankedBars`. To carry more per step, extend the step type (`WaterfallChart<MyStep>`) rather than packing it into `meta`.

Defaults follow the reference cards, so they differ by chart:

- Heights: `Chart` 240, `LineChart` 280, `DotHistogram` 220, `WaffleColumns` 200, `BridgeChart` 360.
- Band padding: 0.2 on a band scale, 0.35 on `BarChart`, 0.45 on `BridgeChart`, 0.3 on `WaffleColumns`.
- Tick counts: 5, and 6 on `DotHistogram`.
- Tones: `InlineBar`, `Meter`, `RangeMeter` and `DotCount` default to `accent` (`RangeMeter`'s reference to `neutral`). `loss` is chosen explicitly.

Ids of points and rows, as `activeId`, `selectedId` and `onSelect` see them:

- `RankedBars`: the index in your data, unless you pass `id`.
- `WaterfallChart`: `'start'`, then `step.id ?? index`, then `'end'`. The end row's `point.datum` is a synthetic `{ label, value }` created on every render, so compare by `id === 'end'`, not by identity.
- `BridgeChart`: `'start'`, then `step.id ?? index`.
- `StripPlot`: `"<series id>:<row id>"`.
- `LineChart`: the x values as strings, so `activeId` takes `'2025'`, not `2025`. For the same reason `1` and `'1'` are the same x, and a repeated x is skipped with a warning. On a time scale they are ISO strings (`'2026-01-04T00:00:00.000Z'`).
- `Heatmap`: `"<row>:<column>"`. Names containing `:` can collide (`a:b` + `c` and `a` + `b:c`), and each row and column name must be unique.

In a `LineChart`, give each series its own `id`. Hover snaps to the nearest x, and one tooltip lists every series there. A forecast that continues the actuals repeats the last actual value, so the two lines join, and the tooltip lists that value once. A series `style` is `'actual'` (solid), `'forecast'` (dashed, hollow dots) or `'scenario'` (dashed, green).
